warmup.q: A network has 100,000 users who follow 50 accounts each, so the average account has about 50 followers. You precompute timelines: every new post is copied into the timeline of each of its author's followers. Which number decides whether every post can reach all of its followers within 5 seconds?
options: The total number of follows, about 5 million
The follower count of the most-followed account
How many users are online at once
warmup.why: An average post costs 50 writes, which nobody notices. The deadline is broken by the account with the most followers: in this lesson's network it has 67,725, so each of its posts needs 67,725 writes. At 5,000 writes a second that is 13.5 seconds for one post. The average and the total describe the overall load well, and hide this case completely.

sections.h: Load is a handful of numbers, and the extremes are part of it
sections.html:
Your payment API handles 2,000 requests a second. That sounds like a description of its load, but it can't tell you what will break first. 2,000 card authorizations of 2 KB each are 4 MB a second of small, independent work: one database round trip each, done in milliseconds. 2,000 requests a second from merchants downloading a month of settlement reports, 50 MB each, are 100 GB a second. That needs different machines, a different storage layout and a different design. Same rate, different systems.

So describing load means picking the few numbers that drive the cost of your system. These are its load parameters. They come in a few kinds:

  • rates: requests per second, posts per day, payments per hour at the Black Friday peak;
  • sizes: bytes per request, rows touched per query;
  • ratios: reads per write, the share of reads a cache answers;
  • counts per key: followers per account, payments per merchant, items per order.

Report the peak, not only the average. In 2012 Twitter received about 5,000 tweets a second on an average day and over 12,000 during big events. Its record, in August 2013, was 143,199 tweets in one second, during a Japanese TV showing of the film Castle in the Sky.

With the parameters in hand you can ask the two questions that scaling is about. If one parameter doubles and the machines stay the same, what happens to response time (the percentiles from lesson 2)? And if response time must stay the same, how many more machines do you need? When twice the machines carry twice the load at the same response time, the system has linear scalability. Usually the cost grows faster than that, and later lessons show why.

The last kind of parameter, counts per key, is the one people forget, because its average looks harmless. This lesson follows one system to show why: a social network's home timeline, the list of recent posts by everyone a user follows. It is the best-documented load problem in public, because Twitter, X and Bluesky have published their numbers, and its shape turns up in payments too.

The lab generates a network of 100,000 users who follow 50 accounts each, chosen the way real networks grow: a few accounts attract most of the follows. Here is how many followers each account ends up with:

followers per account  mean 50.8   p50 21   p99 457   p99.9 2,733   max 67,725

The median account has 21 followers. The most popular one is followed by two thirds of all users, over 1,300 times the average. Every design in this lesson costs about the same for the median account. They differ on that last number.

try.title: Describe the load of a generated network
steps: From the labs folder, run the demo below. It builds the lab's skewed follow graph (100,000 users, seed 42) and prints its load parameters first.
Before you look at the second line of numbers, predict the maximum number of accounts one user follows. Ordinary users follow exactly 50.
Compare the two distributions. Which one is skewed, and where does its skew come from?

code.title: TimelineCostDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.found.l04.demo import kotlin.math.pow import kotlin.random.Random // Prices three home-timeline designs on a skewed follow graph of 100,000 users. // Run from the labs folder: // ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.found.l04.demo.TimelineCostDemoKt --console=plain -q // ./gradlew :sim:demo -Pmain=sfz.found.l04.demo.TimelineCostDemoKt --console=plain -q -Pargs='5000 60' // The first argument is the hybrid's celebrity threshold (followers), the second the number of // timeline reads per post. Everything is counted, not timed, so the output is the same on every machine. const val USERS = 100_000 const val WRITES_PER_SECOND = 5_000.0 // what the fan-out workers can do together const val DEADLINE_SECONDS = 5.0 // a post should reach every follower within this const val REASONABLE_LIMIT = 2_000 // Bluesky's rule for heavy followers fun main(args: Array<String>) { val threshold = args.getOrNull(0)?.toInt() ?: (WRITES_PER_SECOND * DEADLINE_SECONDS).toInt() val readsPerPost = args.getOrNull(1)?.toDouble() ?: 60.0 val followees = skewedGraph(USERS) val followers = IntArray(USERS) for (list in followees) for (f in list) followers[f]++ val follows = followees.map { it.size } println("load parameters of the network") println(" users %,d".format(USERS)) println(" follow edges %,d".format(follows.sum().toLong())) describe(" followers per account ", followers.toList()) describe(" follows per account ", follows) println() val celebrity = BooleanArray(USERS) { followers[it] > threshold } val keep = DoubleArray(USERS) { minOf(REASONABLE_LIMIT.toDouble() / maxOf(follows[it], 1), 1.0) } // writes caused by one post of each author, and lookups caused by one read of each reader val pullWrites = DoubleArray(USERS) { 1.0 } val pullReads = DoubleArray(USERS) { follows[it].toDouble() } val pushWrites = DoubleArray(USERS) { followers[it].toDouble() } val pushReads = DoubleArray(USERS) { 1.0 } val hybridWrites = DoubleArray(USERS) val hybridReads = DoubleArray(USERS) { 1.0 } for (reader in 0 until USERS) for (author in followees[reader]) { if (celebrity[author]) hybridReads[reader] += 1.0 // merged at read time else hybridWrites[author] += keep[reader] // fanned out, maybe sampled } for (author in 0 until USERS) if (celebrity[author]) hybridWrites[author] = 1.0 println(" writes per post lookups per read work per post slowest") val reads = if (readsPerPost % 1.0 == 0.0) "%,.0f".format(readsPerPost) else "%.1f".format(readsPerPost) println("design mean max mean max (%s reads) delivery".format(reads)) row("fan-out on read", pullWrites, pullReads, readsPerPost) row("fan-out on write", pushWrites, pushReads, readsPerPost) row("hybrid > %,d".format(threshold), hybridWrites, hybridReads, readsPerPost) println() println("celebrities (more than %,d followers): %d accounts".format(threshold, celebrity.count { it })) println("work per post = writes per post + reads per post x lookups per read") println("slowest delivery = most writes one post needs / %,.0f writes per second, with an empty queue".format(WRITES_PER_SECOND)) } fun row(name: String, writes: DoubleArray, reads: DoubleArray, readsPerPost: Double) { val w = writes.average() val r = reads.average() println("%-17s %,8.1f %,9.0f %,10.1f %,8.0f %,14.0f %,12.1f s".format( name, w, writes.max(), r, reads.max(), w + readsPerPost * r, writes.max() / WRITES_PER_SECOND)) } fun describe(label: String, values: List<Int>) { val s = values.sorted() fun p(q: Double) = s[((s.size - 1) * q).toInt()] println("%s mean %.1f p50 %,d p99 %,d p99.9 %,d max %,d".format( label, values.average(), p(0.5), p(0.99), p(0.999), s.last())) } /** The lab's FollowGraph.skewed: user 0 is the most popular account; the last 20 users follow 4,000 each. */ fun skewedGraph(size: Int, followsPerUser: Int = 50, heavyUsers: Int = 20, heavyFollows: Int = 4_000, exponent: Double = 0.8, seed: Long = 42): Array<IntArray> { val cdf = DoubleArray(size) var total = 0.0 for (i in 0 until size) { total += 1.0 / (i + 1.0).pow(exponent); cdf[i] = total } val random = Random(seed) return Array(size) { user -> val want = if (user >= size - heavyUsers) heavyFollows else followsPerUser val picked = HashSet<Int>(want * 2) while (picked.size < want) { var target = cdf.binarySearch(random.nextDouble() * total) if (target < 0) target = -target - 1 if (target != user) picked += target.coerceAtMost(size - 1) } picked.toIntArray() } }

sections.h: Fan-out on read: every timeline is a query
sections.html:
Start with the simplest design. Store each post once, next to its author, and build a timeline when someone asks for it. In SQL, with a posts table and a follows table:

SELECT p.post_id, p.author_id, p.body
FROM follows f
JOIN posts p ON p.author_id = f.followee_id
WHERE f.follower_id = :me
ORDER BY p.created_at DESC
LIMIT 50;

The database finds every account :me follows, reads the recent posts of each one and merges them. Posting is as cheap as it gets: one row. A read costs one lookup for every account followed, 50 in the lab's network. When one request causes many requests behind it, that is fan-out, and the number of requests it causes is the fan-out factor. Here the fan-out happens when someone reads, so this design is called fan-out on read.

Now put in realistic load. The model in Designing Data-Intensive Applications uses round numbers: 500 million posts a day (about 5,800 a second), 200 follows per user on average, and 10 million users online who refresh their timeline every 5 seconds. That is 2 million timeline queries a second, each looking up about 200 lists: 400 million lookups a second. For the average user. A user who follows 4,000 accounts makes every one of their reads cost 4,000 lookups.

The cost isn't only work. A read that fans out to 200 lookups has to wait for the slowest of them, and lesson 2 showed that fan-out makes the tail the common case. If each lookup is slow 1% of the time, a read is slow unless all 200 are fast: 1 − 0.99^200, so about 87% of reads hit at least one slow lookup.

Fan-out on read is still the right design when reads are rare or unpredictable. Twitter's search worked this way: a tweet was written once into one index server, and a search asked every server and merged the answers. Nobody can precompute the answer to a search nobody has typed yet. A home timeline is different. It is the same question, asked again and again, by every user, every few seconds.

try.title: Price fan-out on read
steps: Run the demo again (or scroll up to your last run) and find the fan-out on read row.
Predict before you look: the mean and the maximum lookups per read. Which user is behind the maximum?
The work per post column adds one post's writes to the lookups of 60 reads, roughly Twitter's 2012 ratio of reads to posts. Note it down for the next section.
try.expect:
writes per post     lookups per read   work per post     slowest
design                mean       max       mean      max   (60 reads)      delivery
fan-out on read        1.0         1       50.8    4,000          3,048          0.0 s

Every post costs exactly 1 write. The mean read costs 50.8 lookups, one per follow. The maximum, 4,000, is one of the heavy users. work per post is 1 + 60 × 50.8 = 3,048. Delivery is instant, because a new post is visible to the next read with no extra work.

refs.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition (chapter 2 has the timeline model)

sections.h: Fan-out on write: do the work once, when the post arrives
sections.html:
Turn it around. Keep a precomputed timeline for every user: a list of post ids, newest first. When Ana posts, the service looks up her followers and inserts the new post id into each follower's timeline. A read is now one lookup of one list that is already merged and sorted. This design is fan-out on write.

The precomputed timeline is a materialized view, derived data from lesson 1: you could throw every timeline away and rebuild it from the posts and the follows. It exists only to make reads cheap, and you pay for it on every write. A post costs one write per follower of its author.

In the book's model that is 5,800 posts a second × 200 followers, about 1.16 million timeline writes a second, against 400 million lookups for fan-out on read: roughly 345 times less work. Why such a gap? Look at a single author. Fan-out on write charges one write per follower each time the author posts. Fan-out on read charges one lookup per follower each time a follower reads. The follower count is the same on both sides, so per author the question is just which happens more often, posting or reading. Users read their timelines far more often than their friends post, so fan-out on write wins for nearly everyone.

It also handles spikes well. If 150,000 posts arrive in one second, the fan-out work goes into a queue and drains over the next minutes. Posts appear a little late; reads stay fast.

Twitter ran this design in 2012, as Raffi Krikorian described it at QCon that year. Home timelines lived in Redis, an in-memory store, capped at 800 entries per user and kept in 3 copies. The service took about 300,000 timeline reads a second against about 5,000 new tweets. The goal was to deliver a tweet to every follower within 5 seconds, and reaching 1 million followers took about 3.5 seconds.

Now take one author with 31 million followers, as Lady Gaga had then. One of her tweets is 31 million writes. At the rate that reached 1 million followers in 3.5 seconds, that is about 108 seconds with the fan-out workers to itself, and the talk reported deliveries of up to 5 minutes. The workers take posts from a queue, so the posts that arrive behind it wait as well: a post from an account with 200 followers can't start until the 31 million writes ahead of it are done. That is the celebrity problem, a hot key on the write side. The average post is cheap; one account's posts are each a 31-million-write job.

try.title: Price fan-out on write
steps: Find the fan-out on write row in the demo output.
Predict the slowest delivery: the demo's fan-out workers do 5,000 timeline writes a second, and you know the most-followed account from the first Try it.
Compare work per post with the fan-out on read row.
try.expect:
design                mean       max       mean      max   (60 reads)      delivery
fan-out on write      50.8    67,725        1.0        1            111         13.5 s

Writes per post average 50.8, the mean follower count, but one account's posts cost 67,725 writes. At 5,000 writes a second that post takes 67,725 / 5,000 = 13.5 s to reach its last follower, even with an empty queue. Total work per post drops from 3,048 to 111 (50.8 + 60 × 1). So fan-out on write is 27 times cheaper overall and still misses a 5-second target because of one account.

refs.title: Raffi Krikorian, Timelines at Scale (QCon San Francisco 2012)
High Scalability: The architecture Twitter uses to deal with 150M active users

sections.h: The extremes decide: celebrities, heavy followers and the hybrid
sections.html:
The averages say fan-out on write. The extremes say it can't be the whole answer. There are two extremes, one on each side, and each gets its own fix.

The first is the celebrity. Don't fan out accounts with more than some number of followers. Store their posts once, in their own list, as fan-out on read does, and merge them into a follower's timeline when the follower reads. A read then costs one lookup for the precomputed timeline plus one for each celebrity the reader follows. Twitter's 2012 talk described this plan: stop fanning out the very largest accounts and merge them at read time.

Where should the line go? Work it out from the deadline. If the fan-out workers do W writes a second and a post must reach everyone within d seconds, no account with more than W × d followers can be fanned out in time. The demo's workers do 5,000 writes a second and the target is 5 seconds, so the threshold is 25,000 followers. Five accounts in the network are above it. Merging them makes the slowest delivery 4.7 s, and a read now costs 3.1 lookups on average instead of 1. Total work per post goes up, from 111 to 235. In this model the hybrid does more work in total and buys a deadline it can actually meet. (The model also charges for every follower's reads. In a real network many of a celebrity's followers won't open the app before a post scrolls out of their 800 entries, so the copies written for them are wasted work that the hybrid avoids.)

The second extreme is the heavy follower, who follows thousands of accounts and so receives a write for every post any of them makes. Bluesky described its fix in February 2025. Its timelines lived in ScyllaDB, a distributed database, one partition per user, for about 32 million users, and one timeline write took about 600 µs. Users who followed hundreds of thousands of accounts made the machines that held their timelines hot. The fix drops writes on purpose: a user receives a share of their timeline writes equal to min(2000 / follows, 1). Follow 4,000 accounts and half the writes are skipped; follow 8,000 and three quarters are. Nobody reads 8,000 accounts' posts anyway, so they see a fair sample. Fan-out for large accounts went from 5 to 10 minutes to under 10 seconds, and the p99 time to fan out a full post fell by over 96%.

The product can change the load as well. In 2023 X published the code behind its For You timeline. It is no longer "everyone I follow, newest first". Each request gathers about 1,500 candidate posts, roughly half from accounts the user follows and half from accounts they don't, then ranks them with a machine-learning model, and a service called Home Mixer puts the timeline together. Much of that work happens when the user reads, because the ranking depends on the user and the moment.

So here is the method this lesson teaches. Name the load parameters. Find which extreme dominates the cost. Precompute where reads dominate. Then handle each extreme separately, and accept a little imperfection where users can't see it.

try.title: Move the threshold and the read ratio
steps: Run the demo with a threshold of 2,000 followers: add -Pargs='2000 60' to the command. Predict first: what happens to the slowest delivery, and to lookups per read?
Run it with -Pargs='25000 0.5': the same hybrid, but users read only half as often as they post. Which design is cheapest now, and why?
Find the hybrid's mean writes per post with a threshold of 1,000,000 (-Pargs='1000000 60'), where nobody is a celebrity. It is below fan-out on write's 50.8. What removed those writes?
try.expect:
Threshold 2,000:

hybrid > 2,000        41.0     1,978       10.4      157            663          0.4 s
celebrities (more than 2,000 followers): 157 accounts

Delivery drops to 0.4 s, but 157 accounts are now merged at read time, so a read costs 10.4 lookups on average and up to 157. A lower threshold buys faster delivery with more expensive reads.

At 0.5 reads per post, work per post is 26 for fan-out on read against 51 for fan-out on write and 50 for the hybrid: when users read less often than they post, fan-out on read is cheaper. At a threshold of 1,000,000 the hybrid's mean is 50.4 writes, not 50.8: the 20 heavy users follow 4,000 accounts each, so the loss factor keeps only half of their writes.

refs.title: Jaz (Bluesky): When imperfect systems are good, actually: Bluesky's lossy timelines
twitter/the-algorithm: the code behind X's For You timeline

analogy: Fan-out on write is a mail room that sorts every letter into each recipient's pigeonhole the moment it arrives, so picking up your mail takes a second. Fan-out on read keeps one pile per sender, and every time you want your mail you go through the piles of everyone you know. The first is clearly better, until one sender mails 31 million people at once and the sorters do nothing else for the rest of the morning. The hybrid puts that sender's letters on a table by the door, and each person who follows them picks up a copy on the way out. The analogy breaks in two places. Copying a post id costs almost nothing compared with copying a letter. And no mail room would throw away three quarters of someone's mail on purpose, which is exactly what Bluesky does for people who follow 8,000 accounts.
world: Your ledger is the system of record, and the merchant dashboard shows each merchant's current balance. You can compute the balance on read, with a SUM over the merchant's ledger entries (fan-out on read), or keep a balance row that every new payment updates (fan-out on write, a materialized view). The second is right for almost every merchant. Then a ticketing merchant opens sales for a big concert and takes 3,000 payments a second, every one of them updating the same balance row: that merchant is your celebrity, and every payment waits for the row lock. The same skew hits Kafka if you key the payments topic by merchant id, because one partition gets that merchant's whole traffic. The fixes are the ones from this lesson: treat the extreme key separately (split its balance into several sub-rows that a read adds up, or compute it from a snapshot plus recent entries), and describe your load per key, as payments per merchant at p50, p99 and max, not just payments per second.
mistake: Sizing a design from averages. Someone measures the mean number of payments per merchant, or followers per account, finds it small, and builds the design around it. The system then breaks on its first big key: a celebrity post that takes minutes to fan out, a hot merchant that serializes every write on one row, one Kafka partition with ten times the traffic of the others. People make this mistake because averages are what dashboards show by default. The fix is to describe every per-key load parameter as a distribution (p50, p99, max), work out what your design costs for the largest key, and decide in advance what happens to keys past a threshold.

compare.title: The same timeline, built at read time and at write time

a.label: fan-out on read
a.title: on every read: one lookup per account followed
a.html: -- a post is one INSERT into posts -- a read builds the timeline: SELECT p.post_id, p.author_id, p.body FROM follows f JOIN posts p ON p.author_id = f.followee_id WHERE f.follower_id = :me ORDER BY p.created_at DESC LIMIT 50;

b.label: fan-out on write
b.title: Redis lists, the way Twitter kept timelines in 2012
b.html:
# on every post by author A: one write per follower
for f in followers(A):
    LPUSH timeline:f <post id>     # newest at the front
    LTRIM timeline:f 0 799         # keep 800 entries

# on every read: one lookup
LRANGE timeline:me 0 49

compare.note: Both return the 50 newest posts by the accounts :me follows. The query on the left does its work every time someone reads, and its cost grows with how many accounts the reader follows. The loop on the right does its work once per post, and its cost grows with how many followers the author has. LTRIM is why a precomputed timeline stays bounded: old entries fall off the end, and a user who scrolls past them falls back to a slower path.

worked.title: Price both designs at the book's model numbers and pick a threshold

steps.say: Write down the load parameters. The model: 500 million posts a day, 200 follows (and so 200 followers) per user on average, 10 million users online, each refreshing every 5 seconds.
Fan-out on read pays per read: one lookup per account followed.
Fan-out on write pays per post: one write per follower. Reads become one lookup each.

Check the extremes. Suppose the fan-out tier is sized for the average, about 1.2 million writes a second, and a post must reach everyone in 5 seconds. One post from an account with 100 million followers then needs almost a minute and a half, and every post behind it waits.
Set the celebrity threshold from the deadline: the lab's celebrityThreshold is throughput times deadline. Accounts above 6 million followers are merged at read time; everyone else is fanned out.
steps.code: fun celebrityThreshold(writesPerSecond: Double, deadlineSeconds: Double): Long = floor(writesPerSecond * deadlineSeconds).toLong() celebrityThreshold(1_200_000.0, 5.0) // 6,000,000 followers

lab.title: Push, pull and the hybrid
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. All 9 fail with NotImplementedError. No Docker is needed: everything is counted, not timed.
Read Timelines.kt. Work counts writes and lookups, and FanOutOnRead is the finished reference design. The tests check your timelines against it, so read how it merges.
In Designs.kt, write FanOutOnWrite: one ArrayDeque per user, newest first, trimmed to cap. Count one write per follower and one lookup per read.

Write lossFactor, then Hybrid. Celebrities are stored once; everyone else is fanned out, except the writes that sample(postId, follower) says to drop for heavy followers. A read is one lookup plus one per celebrity followed.

In Delivery.kt, write deliverySeconds (one FIFO queue in virtual time) and celebrityThreshold. Run the tests until all 9 pass, including the jqwik property that checks all three designs give every user the same timeline.
hints: Post ids grow with time, so addFirst keeps a timeline sorted newest first. take(limit) on an ArrayDeque gives you the read.
Precompute in the Hybrid constructor which followees of each user are celebrities. Then a read doesn't have to scan all follows to find the few lists to merge.
In the hybrid, merge timeline.take(limit) with recent(celebrityPosts, limit) for each celebrity, then sortedDescending().take(limit). Merging more than limit from each list never changes the answer.
For deliverySeconds, keep one variable: the time at which the queue is next free. A post starts at max(arrival, queueFreeAt).
If the property test fails, it prints the seed and the user. Rerun with that seed in your head: a celebrity threshold of 0 makes every author with a follower a celebrity, which is a good edge case.

drill.title: The hybrid's read path from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write homeTimeline for the hybrid: the user's precomputed timeline (newest first, in timelines[user]), the celebrities they follow (celebritiesFollowed[user]), each celebrity's posts oldest first in celebrityPosts. Count the lookups and return the newest limit ids.

answer.html: override fun homeTimeline(user: Int, limit: Int): List<Long> { work.lookups++ // the precomputed part val merged = ArrayList<Long>(timelines[user].take(limit)) for (celebrity in celebritiesFollowed[user]) { work.lookups++ // one list per celebrity followed merged += recent(celebrityPosts[celebrity] ?: emptyList(), limit) } return merged.sortedDescending().take(limit) }

recap: Load is described by a few load parameters: rates, sizes, ratios and counts per key. Report peaks and distributions, not only averages.
Fan-out on read stores a post once and does the work on every read: one lookup per account followed. It suits rare or unpredictable reads, like search.
Fan-out on write keeps a precomputed timeline per user, a materialized view, and pays one write per follower. Per author it wins whenever followers read more often than the author posts.
The extremes break each design: a celebrity post is millions of writes that delay every post behind it; a heavy follower makes reads, or writes, expensive.
Hybrids handle the extremes separately: merge accounts above W × deadline followers at read time, and sample writes for heavy followers, as Bluesky's min(2000 / follows, 1) does.

explain.prompt: A colleague asks why a social network that precomputes every user's timeline would still merge some posts when the user reads. Explain it with numbers.
explain.answer: Precomputing means every post is copied into each follower's timeline, so a post costs one write per follower and a read costs one lookup. For the average account that is a great deal, because people read far more often than their friends post. But the cost of a post is its author's follower count, and that count is extremely skewed. An account with 31 million followers needs 31 million writes per post. If the fan-out workers do about 285,000 writes a second, that's well over a minute and a half per post, and every ordinary post queued behind it waits too. So accounts above a threshold (the workers' writes per second times the delivery deadline) are stored once and merged into a follower's timeline at read time. That makes reads a bit more expensive, one extra lookup per celebrity followed, and keeps delivery within the deadline for everyone else.

deeper.html:
Weighted costs. This lesson counted a write and a lookup as one unit each. They aren't equal in practice: Twitter pipelined timeline inserts in batches of thousands, while a fan-out-on-read lookup is a random read that the reader waits for. Give them weights, c_w per write and c_l per lookup, and the per-author rule becomes: fan out on write when posts × c_w < reads × c_l. The follower count still cancels. What doesn't cancel is who waits: fan-out on read puts the cost on the reader's response time, fan-out on write puts it on delivery time, which a queue can absorb.

Caching the extremes. Bluesky's rule needs each user's follow count on every fan-out. Its post says those counts, for users who follow many accounts, are kept in a Redis sorted set reloaded every 30 seconds, and that without the cache the lookups would add over a million reads a second to the primary database. Even the fix for one extreme had to be designed around another load parameter.

Why the lab samples with a hash. sample(postId, follower) turns the pair into a fixed number in [0, 1), so the same post is kept or dropped for the same follower every time you run the code, and the tests can be exact. A production system could use a random number, but a deterministic one also means a retried fan-out job drops the same writes, instead of filling in some it skipped the first time.

The opposite pattern, on purpose. Twitter's search index (Earlybird, a modified Lucene index held in RAM) stored each tweet on one machine and asked every machine at query time: fan-out on read, because nobody can precompute the answer to a search that hasn't been typed. Most large systems use both patterns, chosen per feature from that feature's load parameters.
